payload.text: Audit 2026-09-15: core/cursor.ts exportEvents exports every envelope-valid event, and client/push.ts pushes that stream without event-type privacy filtering. The hook intentionally excludes self-recording git/sofar commands; CommandRunPayload currently carries only cmd, and MCP rejections return errors without outcome events. A miner cannot treat missing outcomes, calls or memory-use evidence as zero, and never-synced diagnostics cannot simply be appended to initiative events.jsonl.

Audit checkpoint: self-improve remains 0/11 with no gating Decisions recorded and no tune/improve commands implemented in main. Priority design findings: (1) proposed miner metrics exceed existing event observability; (2) local-only diagnostics conflict with exporting all events and cannot be stored as disposable derived indexes if they are the only evidence; (3) offline replay validates rendering, not causal model behavior; (4) checksums and writable-worktree diff checks do not isolate the evaluator; (5) proposal approval/application/reversion, durable budgets and an immutable supervisor need explicit contracts; (6) repeated held-out lead gates risk test-set overfitting; (7) compare full improvement-loop cost against matched-budget simpler baselines. Findings are advisory, not new Decisions.

payload.summary:
# self-improve: architecture, research and competitive audit
Date: 2026-09-15. Audit only. Recommendations are not adopted Decisions.

## Verdict
Keep the initiative, but strengthen the evidence and control contracts before implementation. L1 is presently a deterministic diagnostic/proposal system, L2 is an agent-assisted patch-and-evaluate loop, and L3 is a release evaluation process. Calling the whole system zero-model or autonomously self-improving would overstate the plan: L2 uses the operator's agent and inference budget, and changes remain subject to human review.

The most valuable potential advantage is a low-overhead, inspectable improvement process that detects real failures, proposes bounded changes, measures their net benefit on unseen work, and retains the evidence needed to reject or reverse them. Neither automatic harness search nor local event-sourced memory alone establishes novelty.

Scope: all 11 initiative tasks, its current record, dependencies on r1-fixes and bench-refresh, targeted reads of schema, hooks, MCP, exports/sync, indexes, driver and permission contracts, and primary research. Main baseline: 8b4c33c. The implementation worktree's self-improve plan also showed 0/11; no gating Decisions were recorded. No tune/improve CLI implementation was found in the inspected main source. The live r1-fixes worktree was at 9d86222 when inventoried; its implementation was not changed or certified here.

Verification: ran existing cursor.test.ts and client-push.test.ts against main; 25/25 tests passed. These tests check existing event export/import and local mock-cloud sync behavior. They do not test an unimplemented self-improvement loop. No model runs, benchmark cells, candidate launches or publication were performed.

## S1 — The proposed miner cannot measure several promised signals from the existing log
Affected: 1.2, 2.1, 2.2.

Observed code:
- packages/schema/src/events.ts: CommandRunPayload contains only cmd, FileTouchedPayload contains path/op, and memory promotion contains text. These do not carry tool result, cost, render exposure or a reliable memory-use signal.
- packages/engine/src/cli/event.ts: handlePostTool recognizes Edit/MultiEdit/Write/Bash; self-recording git/sofar commands are exempt; unrecognized tools return without recording.
- packages/engine/src/mcp/server.ts: typed rejections return an error result; no outcome event is appended in the catch.
- packages/engine/src/core/index-reach.ts: references are citations found in recorded prose, not proof that an agent read or relied on a memory.
- driver/drive.ts: launches without an attributable registered session can stall without a handoff event. Counting handoff events does not recover all attempts or all stalls.

Consequences:
| Proposed signal | What can be established now | Required interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| Duplicate session starts | Raw event lines can show duplicate starts; fold intentionally removes them from reconstructed sessions. | Inspect valid raw events with correction semantics and classify duplicates separately from corrupt data. |
| Corrections | Correction events and targets are observable. | A correction is not automatically shell mangling, waste, or a defect; changing a legitimate prior decision is different. |
| Stalls | Recorded handoffs/run stops provide some evidence. | Report coverage and unresolved launch gaps; do not equate missing handoffs with successful or absent work. |
| Sofar share of commands/tool calls | Sofar shell commands are intentionally excluded, and MCP/read-only calls are not a complete denominator. | Cannot estimate total bookkeeping share from command_run alone. |
| Historical digest bytes | Today's renderer can render old event prefixes. | That is a simulated digest, not necessarily what the historical agent saw. Historical renderer version, external repo memory, session identity and Git inputs may be missing. |
| Memories never referenced | Some explicit textual citations may be detectable. | Label as no observed citation, never as unused/useless. An agent can follow an injected rule without citing it. |

Define an observability contract before mining: host/tool version, engine version, record/session identity, attempt/tool-call identity, success/error/unknown, capture capability and coverage, and the immutable evidence behind a detector result. Normalize supported adapters and return unavailable for unsupported signals. Do not infer memory usefulness from frequency alone or delete rare standing rules.

Evidence collection must not create another bookkeeping tax. Bound payload size, avoid transcripts by default, coalesce where the host supports it, and measure hook latency, bytes written and model-visible overhead. Share the outcome schema with r1-fixes 2.5 rather than building two collectors.

## S2 — Local-only evidence and durable record truth need different storage contracts
Affected: 1.1, 1.2, 2.1, 2.3.

Confirmed: core/cursor.ts exportEvents includes every envelope-valid event. client/push.ts pushStream exports that stream and filters only by cursor, not privacy classification. A new diagnostics event in initiative events.jsonl therefore reaches the sync/export path. Gitignore does not prevent this.

The existing .sofar/.index design is disposable derived data: deleting it must not change answers. New raw observations that exist nowhere else cannot be put there while claiming they are rebuildable. Conversely, keeping all raw diagnostics in a local-only store creates a limit on cross-machine replay: a shared proposal may have only a sanitized summary or evidence fingerprint, not its full supporting observations.

Before coding, choose and document:
1. Which facts are durable, shareable initiative events.
2. Which raw diagnostics are private, never exported or synced, with explicit retention/deletion rules.
3. Which caches are fully rebuildable.
4. What sanitized evidence is retained for a proposal after local diagnostics expire.
5. Whether every proposal consumer can verify its evidence, or must report evidence unavailable.

A local append-only diagnostic journal, excluded at the actual export/sync boundaries, is one possible design; it requires a scoped exception to the current all-work-state-in-record protocol if it becomes additional truth. Do not create an unacknowledged second source of truth. Keep all new event payload schemas within packages/schema/src.

Redact error text, tool arguments and paths as appropriate before durable storage. is_error and exit code alone are not authoritative semantic test outcomes. Diagnostic recording failure must not turn a successful user operation into a failure or recursively generate an unbounded stream of diagnostic errors. Explicitly test no-write-on-invalid-input behavior if MCP rejection capture changes it.

## S3 — Offline replay is not an improvement experiment
Affected: 2.2, 2.3, 3.3.

Replaying an event prefix can validate deterministic rendering, size, preserved constraints, retrieval ranking and compatibility. It cannot establish that a different digest would cause fewer model turns, fewer decision violations or better code, because changing context changes the agent's subsequent actions. Reusing the original successful trajectory assumes the answer.

Split evidence into:
- Mechanical replay: same versioned inputs, deterministic output; all essential rules and provenance preserved; byte/token budgets and ranking checks.
- Behavioral evaluation: fresh agent sessions given the candidate, against fixed tasks and evaluator, measuring outcomes, full cost and intervention rate.
- Transfer evaluation: previously unseen tasks, preferably additional project/agent families, with the candidate frozen.

Avoid hindsight: replay each candidate only against evidence available before the session being simulated. Reconstruct corrected events and historical state carefully; do not use later memories, later test results or today's repo.md as though they were available then.

Rediscovering the same seven smoke/calibration examples that inspired detector rules is a useful regression test, not independent precision/recall validation. Use a labeled corpus of held-out logs from distinct sessions/projects, negative cases and unknown-coverage cases; freeze labels before testing. Report precision and recall per detector, with counts and confidence/coverage. Fewer false alerts is often more valuable than a single pooled score.

## S4 — Evaluator protection is weaker than the goal requires
Affected: 3.1, 3.2, 3.3.

A checksum and a final diff review do not make an evaluator independent:
- The candidate may read hidden tasks without changing them.
- A test script, package configuration, import path, fixture loader, scoring parser or environment variable can change how an unchanged test file behaves.
- A candidate can modify and restore a file before the final diff.
- A log can claim tests ran even when no evaluator ran.
- The candidate itself may be the sofar binary currently supervising the experiment, allowing it to change how its own result is interpreted.

The driver permission file is explicitly not a sandbox: permissions can be widened by the operator's other settings. A read-only file owned by the same writable environment is not a sufficient isolation claim.

Use a frozen supervisor and evaluator outside the candidate's write/control surface. Pin candidate code, evaluator/config/dependency identity and evaluation inputs; run evaluation independently against a fresh candidate artifact. Separate task instructions that an agent must see from hidden answers/tests it must not see. Capture exit/result artifacts through the trusted runner; do not trust agent-written score summaries.

Protect the whole measurement path, not just hidden-tests/*.ts. Run a known-passing and a deliberately wrong control to verify the evaluator detects success and failure. Deliberately test score forgery, wrapper changes, missing tests, altered fixtures and an attempted hidden-data read using isolated fixtures, not the live held-out benchmark.

No new process isolation framework is assumed by this audit. Pick a mechanism that can actually enforce the stated access boundaries, and describe remaining limits honestly.

## S5 — Proposal adoption, rollback and experiments lack a complete lifecycle
Affected: 2.3, 3.1.

The goal says proposed, not applied, but task 2.3 also says before going live without specifying how approval, application and reversion occur. Distinguish a proposal from an active policy.

A useful candidate record identifies:
- evidence IDs and cutoff, detector/version and coverage;
- target scope: engine version, host, initiative/repo, and settings allowed to change;
- baseline configuration/code fingerprint;
- one bounded change, predicted metric/direction/magnitude, falsifier and evaluation budget;
- candidate/evaluator identities and observed results;
- proposed/evaluated/rejected/approved/applied/reverted/superseded status.

Use append-only transitions and immutable references. Approval binds to the exact evaluated candidate, not a prose description or a mutable branch name. Refuse stale apply when the target baseline changed. Reversion changes current policy using a new event; it does not erase history or undo code side effects already produced while that policy was active.

Repeated tune calls should not keep emitting the same proposal into every digest. Define dry-run as non-mutating, with an explicit persistence action or clearly named separate command. Rate-limit display, cap active suggestions, suppress previously rejected equivalent proposals until evidence materially changes, and expire stale baselines explicitly.

Hysteresis means using different thresholds for adopting versus undoing a setting to avoid oscillation. It still needs minimum evidence, cooldowns and scope rules. Tune one variable at a time initially, then test interactions; otherwise the loop cannot attribute a gain or explain a regression.

Freeze the protected floor: log integrity, session routing, explicit standing constraints, evaluator integrity, permissions and release policy must not be silently weakened because a proxy metric gets cheaper. No automatic increase in authority belongs in the tuning whitelist.

## S6 — Worktree ownership, budgets and stopping need outer-loop guarantees
Affected: 3.1, 3.3.

docs/SPEC.md, Driver, requires one launch directory per run; drive creates no worktree and checks that its working directory uses the same initiative log. Therefore improve can prepare and own a worktree, then invoke drive inside it; drive should not silently acquire worktree-management behavior. Specify how experiment history in that worktree is reconciled back without losing either append-only history.

Pin the supervisor binary, candidate binary/artifact, model/effort and tool environment separately. Do not swap the installed sofar executable under a running benchmark or under the supervisor. Preserve concurrent user changes and never force-clean an unrelated checkout. Handle two improve requests for the same evidence, a lost process, a stale baseline and a partially completed candidate.

Current drive --cost-cap restarts from zero on resume; max-sessions reconstructs from recorded handoffs and misses unattributed launches. Some adapters report no cost, and a per-session timeout is optional. These are documented limits, not suitable outer-loop budget guarantees.

Record a finite experiment budget across every launch, retry, resume and evaluator run; include unattributed failures and unavailable-cost cases. Use available enforceable attempt/time/token bounds with explicit limitations where cost cannot be measured. Bound no-progress retries and candidate count. Stop on exhausted evidence/budget, invariant failure, unavailable verification, repeated no gain, operator stop, or required human judgment. The correct result can be no useful proposal.

Measure amortized value: if search/evaluation/review costs S and the candidate saves d per future task, the simple break-even is S/d tasks for positive d. Include unsuccessful attempts in S. A loop that spends more than its likely future benefit can be technically successful and commercially poor.

## S7 — The release gate needs statistical and lifecycle design
Affected: 4.1, 4.2.

D19 is an existing owner rule and remains unchanged by this audit. It needs a formal measurement contract:
- State metric direction and unit; cheaper/fewer violations are lower-is-better.
- Report absolute outcomes and margins. A preserved negative margin still means sofar is behind.
- Report win, parity, loss or inconclusive with per-rep data and uncertainty.
- A missing/failed competitor run is unavailable, not zero performance.
- Correctness/integrity regressions cannot disappear inside an average gain.
- C6/C7/C8 currently require their deferred addenda; do not mark unmeasured claims as passing.
- Define a noise-floor arm as repeated identical baseline configuration under the same run conditions, not a deliberately weak baseline.
- Treat the full task chain/independent project as the replication unit where sessions/tests are correlated. Three repetitions are initial evidence, not an automatic five-point certification.
- Comparing the observed best of many competitors introduces selection effects; freeze the comparison set and analysis before the runs.

Re-pin competitors at each round boundary, keep them fixed within the round, and rerun the old sofar baseline against that SAME new snapshot. Otherwise competitor/model updates confound the measured improvement from self-improve.

Separate tuning, candidate selection/validation, and release-only held-out evaluation. Repeatedly looking at chain B and fixing failures against it makes it training feedback, even if its files are read-only. Once its feedback steers a candidate, retire it as unseen for subsequent claims or apply an explicitly designed holdout-reuse method. A controlled fresh-holdout schedule is simpler for an initial release.

Any tolerance/non-inferiority interpretation of D19's literal no-shrinking requirement requires an explicit owner Decision. The audit recommends formalizing the rule, not bypassing it. Benchmark results inform a stable-release promotion after testing; they do not retrospectively justify publication.

## S8 — A fair improvement-loop baseline is missing
Affected: 3.3, 4.1.

One manually guided cycle is a feasibility demonstration. It cannot prove sustained self-improvement or superiority to a human engineer. If the candidate agent can read the already-implemented r1-fixes patch, comparing its result to that same human-built fix tests reproduction, not independent discovery.

Evaluate on a frozen loss packet and baseline, with the comparator patch hidden until assessment. Match feedback and total search budget. Useful controls:
1. No change to sofar, rerun to estimate variance.
2. A human using the same loss evidence under a declared effort budget.
3. The same agent fixing the loss directly without the miner/improve orchestration.
4. A simple fixed candidate search or extra task attempts under comparable inference/feedback budgets, with selection performed without hidden-answer access.

Track useful patch yield, confirmed held-out improvement per search budget, time to reviewed patch, review effort, false improvement rate and total regressions. Preserve rejected candidates and their reasons. Demonstrate more than one cycle on different failure classes before claiming that the loop keeps improving itself.

## S9 — Public standing is an outcome to observe, not the optimization target
Affected: 4.3.

Downloads, stars, listings and mentions can reflect publicity, bots, packaging changes and seasonality rather than product quality. They cannot reasonably be guaranteed to rise after every technical release. Keep a separate descriptive report and do not use these metrics to reward code changes or to override quality gates.

Define package/repository identities, source URLs, exact observation windows/time zones, deduplication, missing-data/rate-limit handling and collector version. Fetch failures must not look like popularity declines. Registry presence is categorical; total stars are cumulative; weekly downloads are a flow. Do not average them into an invented industry score.

Reading public metrics is network activity even though it is not telemetry emission. Keep the collector explicit and opt-in/outside the default local engine path; document any change to current network-use contracts. Local diagnostic contents or repo paths must never be sent as search/query parameters. Public standing does not measure private user retention; do not imply it does.

## Task-by-task disposition

| Task | Recommendation | Evidence required before completion |
|---|---|---|
| 1.1 Gating Decisions | Expand to cover truth/storage boundaries, privacy/export policy, experiment authority and data lifetime. | Written contracts precede new schema/code; explicit distinction between durable evidence and disposable caches. |
| 1.2 Capture outcomes | Build once with r1-fixes 2.5, using capability-aware normalization. | Realistic host fixtures, success/error/unknown, dedupe, crash/truncated data, no recursive capture, redaction, bounded overhead and export exclusion. |
| 2.1 tune dry-run | Start with signals the data actually supports. | Deterministic versioned detector output, immutable evidence references, coverage/unavailable flags, read-only behavior, bounded large-log work. |
| 2.2 Miner precision/recall | Keep rediscovery as regression coverage; add independent validation. | Labeled held-out logs, negative/ambiguous cases and per-detector counts; no semantic-cause claims unsupported by evidence. |
| 2.3 Reversible proposals | Specify proposal lifecycle and separate replay from behavioral proof. | No-op repeat runs, stale apply rejection, exact candidate approval, bounded display, stable replay, safe reversal, protected constraints and interaction checks. |
| 3.1 improve controller | Proceed after acceptance, isolation and budget contracts. | One owned worktree/experiment, frozen supervisor, durable attempts/budget, replayable results, no auto-merge, no peer-state clobber, stop/restart recovery. |
| 3.2 Evaluator protection | Broaden from checksum/diff checks to independently controlled evaluation. | Whole measurement path pinned; candidate cannot write evaluator/results or read hidden answers; known-good/bad controls and tampering fixtures. |
| 3.3 First cycle | Call it a pilot; make the baseline independent. | Same initial evidence and budget, comparator solution hidden, full unsuccessful-search cost counted; fresh-task transfer and more cycles before broad claims. |
| 4.1 Lead scoreboard | Formalize D19 rather than assume three reps settle it. | Metric direction, absolute and relative results, variance, missing-arm handling, all claimed addenda, frozen candidate and untouched holdout. |
| 4.2 Re-pin competitors | Keep, with same-round old-sofar control. | Exact versions/config/model/effort; native-state isolation; direct memory competitors for product claims and improvement-loop baselines for algorithm claims. |
| 4.3 Standing snapshot | Keep as a separate descriptive benchmark-owner report. | Public-source provenance, consistent windows, failures distinguished from decline, no diagnostic egress and no causal leadership claim. |

## Research and novelty assessment
Primary sources checked 2026-09-15. Findings below summarize their stated results and scope, not independent validation of every experiment.

- Meta-Harness already searches harness code using experimental feedback. Automatic outer-loop harness improvement is established research, not unique to sofar. [Meta-Harness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.28052).
- LangChain's Better Harness explicitly treats evaluation data as training data for harness optimization and calls for train/test separation. Borrow the feedback discipline; do not treat repeated score chasing as a release proof. [Better Harness](https://www.langchain.com/blog/better-harness-a-recipe-for-harness-hill-climbing-with-evals).
- Karpathy's autoresearch restricts the editable surface and separates fixed evaluation/preparation code from the candidate training code. That is a useful experiment design example, not a ready-made software quality metric or a guarantee of isolation. [autoresearch](https://github.com/karpathy/autoresearch).
- Sakana's DGM documents fake successful tool logs and modification of markers used by a reward detector. This specifically supports independent evaluator/result capture and preserving the experiment lineage. Its reported gains do not predict gains for sofar. [DGM](https://sakana.ai/dgm/).
- Rethinking the Evaluation of Harness Evolution for Agents compares harness evolution with simpler search under comparable inference and feedback budgets and reports limited generalization in its studied setting. It is a direct reason to add matched-budget controls and held-out transfer. The audit does not generalize this into a claim that self-improvement never works. [Paper, revised 2026-08-27](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12227).
- Self-Harness reports held-out improvements for bounded self-edits with a fixed evaluator/model setup. Together with the preceding evaluation critique, this shows that outcomes depend on protocol and task/model scope; the label self-improvement is not evidence. [Self-Harness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.09498).
- Safe Harness Self-Evolution is a September 2026 theoretical preprint separating candidate generation from finite-data certification. Its analysis explains why more candidates need not help when evaluation is the bottleneck and why one successful update does not guarantee another. It is theoretical support for bounded search and explicit no-gain outcomes, not a production guarantee. [Preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.08175).
- Repeated adaptive access can overfit a holdout set even when the underlying samples never change. This supports separating candidate-development feedback from release evaluation and tracking holdout exposure. [Generalization in Adaptive Data Analysis and Holdout Reuse](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.02629).

The earlier r1-fixes audit identified Beads, PROJECTMEM, OpenMemory and Letta as relevant product comparators. For this initiative, add comparison against improvement METHODS, not just memory products: direct repair by the same agent and matched-budget simple search are necessary to show the miner/controller adds value.

## Recommended build order and first proof
1. Write the shared outcome/storage/authority contracts with r1-fixes.
2. Build a small local miner for duplicate starts, precisely classified tool failures and attributable stalls; keep unsupported measures unavailable.
3. Validate detectors on independent logs and keep suggestions in shadow mode, with no automatic policy changes.
4. Define durable proposal application, independent verification, frozen supervisor and experiment budgets.
5. Run a bounded pilot on one independently chosen loss, then a second distinct loss. Preserve human review.
6. Compare against matched-budget baselines, test fresh-task transfer, and only then connect it to a stable-release gate.
7. Keep public standing in a separate report.

Suggested acceptance targets must be frozen before building/running; this audit does not invent numerical expected gains. The present self-improve tasks contain few explicit measurable predictions despite the wider improvement program's D10 discipline. Each capability needs a defined success metric, baseline, falsifier and budget, including the ability to report insufficient evidence.

The first convincing deliverable is not an agent endlessly rewriting sofar. It is a small, repeatable demonstration that a recorded failure led to an independently verified improvement on new work, at lower total cost than a simpler repair process, with a complete rejection/reversion trail.

## Handoff
No code, plan statuses, standing Decisions, benchmark freezes, installs or release actions changed. Audit findings are stored in the main checkout's self-improve record; reconcile this history through the normal append-only process if implementation proceeds in a separate worktree. Do not reinterpret the findings as owner approval for new authority, new storage contracts or a relaxed D19 gate.

payload.because:
Verified against the repo:
- record-hygiene D1 exempts git and sofar commands from the record, so bookkeeping share cannot be mined from events.
- The exporter includes every valid event, and events.jsonl is committed to git, so "local-only" needs a separate store.
The research shows automatic harness loops are not unique and often don't beat simpler search. The risk is better-looking scores without a better product, so the credible edge is a small, auditable loop proven against a direct-fix baseline on unseen work, with its full cost counted.
payload.chose:
Adopt the Codex audit (codex-self-improve-audit-20260915-01) plus these additions, ruled by the run owner 2026-09-15.
AUDIT: (1) signals that aren't captured are reported as UNKNOWN, never guessed; capture is defined first. (2) Private diagnostics are separated from shareable history AT the storage/export boundary. (3) A frozen evaluator runs outside the candidate's control and protects scoring, fixtures and result capture, not just test files. (4) Offline replay proves only context size and information preservation; quality, cost and behaviour need fresh agent runs. (5) Approval binds to an exact tested candidate hash; stale applications are rejected; rejection and reversal history is kept. (6) A durable spend ledger counts every attempt, retry and evaluation across restarts. (7) Development feedback is separated from release evaluation; a held-out workload whose failures guide a fix is retired. (8) The loop must beat a BASELINE: the same agent directly fixing the same loss with equal feedback and budget (Meta-Harness / Better Harness exist, and arXiv 2607.12227 found harness evolution doesn't consistently beat simpler search at equal budget). (9) Downloads and stars stay out of technical gates.
ADDITIONS: (A) The first loop is DEVELOPER-SIDE: bench, loss study, bounded fix, held-out proof, run on our benchmark infrastructure. In-product L1 adaptation inside users' repos is deferred until that loop has repeated wins, which removes privacy and sync risk from the early phases. (B) Outcome capture has ONE owner: self-improve 1.2 defines the schema and private store, and r1-fixes 2.5 consumes it. (C) Improvement claims are NET of the whole improvement cost (fix attempts plus evaluations). (D) Autonomy expands only after 3 consecutive cycles beat the direct-fix baseline on unseen work.
DIFFERENTIATOR: every improvement's benefit, cost, evidence and reversal path is inspectable in the record.

Developer-side first: benchmark → loss study → bounded fix → held-out proof, beating an equal-budget direct-fix baseline net of full cost. In-product local adaptation only after repeated wins; private diagnostics never enter events.jsonl, git, export or sync.

Signal availability map: every promised signal marked capturable or UNKNOWN with its reason (e.g. sofar and git commands are hook-exempt per record-hygiene D1); consumers report unknown, never guess
`sofar tune --dry-run` detects only well-supported failure types (duplicate session starts, corrections, stalls, formatter friction) and prints unknown for the rest
Precision and recall against the manual smoke and round-1 loss-study rows before any suggestion is trusted

Suggestions only: approval bound to an exact candidate hash, stale applications rejected, rejection and reversal history kept; offline replay limited to context-size and information-preservation checks
Frozen evaluator outside the candidate's control: runner, hidden tests, fixtures, scoring and result capture live in a separate repo and process the candidate cannot write

payload.chose:
1.1(a) — the outcome-capture SCHEMA contract, gating 1.2 and r1-fixes 2.5.
(1) Two shapes, one home. Both the durable outcome fields (event payloads) and the private diagnostics ROW shape live in packages/schema/src — event payloads in events.ts, the row shape in its own file (e.g. diagnostics.ts), exported from the package entry. Nothing in packages/engine defines or widens either shape.
(2) The split rule. DURABLE (an event in events.jsonl) is a fact the next session on ANY machine needs to resume, at the granularity a human write-back already states: that a command ran and whether it exited ok, that a file was touched. Concretely 1.2 may add OPTIONAL fields to the existing mechanical payloads — command_run gains exit status and an ok flag; file_touched gains an ok flag — and nothing more. Commit facts stay derived from git (commit-attribution: recorded in git, derived from git, never in the record), so r1-fixes 2.5's "commits with task-id prefix" is a read, not a capture. PRIVATE (a diagnostics row, never an event) is everything at tool-call granularity or richer: error text and stderr tails, is_error from the host, PostToolUseFailure payloads, MCP typed-error rejections, hook latency, bytes injected, digest size, memory citation signals, tool names and counts including read-only tools and self-recording git/sofar commands.
(3) Rows are structurally not events. A row carries no ulid `id` and its `kind` is never a member of EVENT_TYPES, so validateEnvelope rejects it by construction; a test pins this. The record may reference diagnostics only by opaque row id, content hash or aggregate count — never by content.
(4) Additive only. New durable fields are optional; an engine that predates them folds the event unchanged (the fold counts command_run and never reads cmd — that stays true). A consumer that finds a field absent reports UNKNOWN for it, never a default (1.3 owns the availability map).
(5) Redaction precedes storage on both sides: command text only through redactCommand; error text clipped to a fixed byte bound and redacted; no tool arguments, no transcripts, no absolute paths outside the clone root by default.
payload.over: (a) A single rich `tool_outcome` event type in events.jsonl carrying exit code, is_error and error text — the audit's original 1.2 shape. (b) Keeping the row shape inside packages/engine next to the store code, since only the engine reads it. (c) A new `test_result` event that names pass/fail semantically.
payload.rule: Outcome capture adds only OPTIONAL exit/ok fields to command_run and file_touched in packages/schema/src; every richer observation is a diagnostics row whose shape also lives in packages/schema/src, never validates as an event envelope, and is referenced from the record only by id, hash or count.

payload.chose:
1.1(b) — the diagnostics STORAGE BOUNDARY, gating 1.2.
(1) Location: OUTSIDE the repo. Private diagnostics live under `~/.local/state/sofar/diagnostics/<sha256(clone-path)>/` (XDG_STATE_HOME-aware), keyed exactly like the sync cursors in sync-client D2's storage triad. Never under `.sofar/`, never under the clone root; the path resolver refuses a target inside the repo and a test pins that refusal.
(2) Form: an append-only JSONL journal of rows in the packages/schema/src row shape, one file per initiative slug, each row stamped with schema version, engine version, clone hash, initiative, session id, timestamp, kind, host tool and version when known. Rotated at a per-clone byte cap; rows older than 90 days deleted on the next write; a purge subcommand wipes the clone's store. Exact cap and names are settled in 1.2 against measured row sizes.
(3) Not truth, not derived. The store is a THIRD class next to events.jsonl (truth) and .sofar/.index (derived, disposable): raw observations that exist nowhere else and are NOT rebuildable, so it never goes in .index (record-index D1 forbids irrebuildable data there) and never claims disposability. Its loss costs evidence, never record correctness — nothing the fold, the projections or the digest's byte-stable block depends on may read it.
(4) The exemption does not reach it. record-hygiene D1 exempts git and sofar commands from the RECORD because the append would keep the tree from settling; the store is outside the tree, so exempt commands and read-only MCP calls ARE counted there (command token only, redacted). This recovers the bookkeeping-share denominator the audit (S1) called unmeasurable — with coverage limits 1.3 must state: hooks fire only on Edit|Write|MultiEdit|Bash, MCP calls are counted by the server itself, and Read/Grep/other tools are never observed.
(5) Best-effort per BD22, and never recursive: a failed row write never fails the user's tool call, never appends an event, and is never itself recorded as a diagnostic. MCP typed-error rejections write a row and still append nothing to the record (no-write-on-invalid-input is pinned by test).
(6) Enforced at the boundary by tests: with a seeded store carrying a sentinel under a fake XDG_STATE_HOME, exportEvents, exportNDJSON, `sofar export`, pushStream (mock fetch) and pullStream/importNDJSON must move zero bytes of it; a row must fail validateEnvelope; a row write in a temp repo must leave `git status` clean.
(7) Sanitized evidence: a proposal (2.3) may carry row ids, hashes and counts into the record as its evidence; when the rows have expired the consumer reports evidence unavailable, never reconstructs it.

payload.because: Audit S3 asks for held-out logs from distinct sessions/projects, negative and unknown-coverage cases, frozen labels, per-detector counts. Labels must be semantic (a correction that was a change of mind is not a loss) or precision is tautological for event-type detectors, and they must come from transcripts or recall can only find what the detector's own rule finds (e.g. calib-1's biome.json edit left 0 file_touched events). Precision gates, not recall, because 2.3 turns findings into suggestions and a false alert costs trust; recall is reported so blind spots stay visible. The corpus stays out of sofar's git because round 1 is live and bench content is unpublished; hashes in the record make any later edit detectable. No corpus has capture-era rows or ok fields, so tool_failure / mcp_rejections / bookkeeping_share / injection_bytes cannot be validated here and stay untrusted by construction.
payload.chose: 2.2 measurement protocol, pre-registered before any label exists. CORPUS (snapshot outside the repo at ~/IO/bench-cells/tune-eval-2.2, local git 0ae9e72, manifest sha256 2c4bf41d…, rubric sha256 44727e8d…): REGRESSION split = the 9 smoke/calib bench cells with records (visible when 2.1 was designed — rediscovery only, never counted toward trust); VALIDATION split = round-1 rep-1 claude-sofar, codex-sofar, cursor-sofar (S1–S10 complete, unseen); OPERATOR split = this repo's 56 initiatives, events strictly before 01M2K1JCAKZT77FM8HEFP3HB0Z (distinct project, real sessions). LABELS: blind subagent labelers who may not read tune.ts, signals.ts, their tests, SPEC or the self-improve record, nor run sofar; they label semantic failure instances (duplicate_registration, record_correction, stall, formatter_config, mcp_rejection, sofar_cli_failure) from transcripts plus the snapshot, loss/benign/ambiguous, evidence by event id; label files are hashed into the record BEFORE replay. REPLAY: detect() bundled from b219616, rows=[] (no capture-era rows exist in any unit), signals from each unit's own settings. SCORING: finding↔label by shared event id and mapped type; TP = matches a loss; FP = matches only benign or nothing; ambiguous-only excluded and counted; FN = loss with record events in a unit where the detector ran and no finding shares an id; loss with no record event = FN-untraceable, reported apart (two recalls); loss in a unit where the detector is UNKNOWN = unobserved, never FN. COVERAGE VIOLATION = a detector prints a number on a unit whose corpus cannot contain its source while labels show ≥1 loss of its type. GATE: TRUSTED for 2.3 iff on validation ∪ operator TP+FP ≥ 5, precision ≥ 0.80, Wilson 95% lower bound ≥ 0.50, and no coverage violation on any split; otherwise UNTRUSTED naming the failing clause (insufficient evidence is not failure).
payload.over: Scoring detectors by rediscovering the smoke preview rows (audit S3: regression, not validation); labeling with the detector's own rule or after seeing its output; committing bench-cell logs and labels into sofar's pushed git; a single pooled score across detectors and splits; a gate on recall.

payload.because: The audit's S5 asks for a complete lifecycle with immutable references, approval bound to the exact evaluated candidate, stale applies refused, suppression of rejected equivalents, minimum evidence and a protected floor. A loss row is what the trusted detector can honestly support: `corrections` proves that the record was fixed N times, not why, and 2.2 measured that it misses half of them — a number that belongs on the row the operator reads. Phase 3 consumes approved rows, which is what 3.4 ("first manual cycle on one round-1 loss row") needs from Phase 2.
payload.chose: 2.3 contract, settled before code. (1) A SUGGESTION IS A LOSS ROW, never a fix: {candidate hash, signal, scope = one initiative, evidence ids, count, corpus cutoff, engine version, detector report version, trust}. It names no cause and proposes no change; the fix, its predicted gain, its falsifier and its budget belong to Phase 3. (2) TRUST TRAVELS WITH IT: a candidate can only come from a detector the 2.2 protocol marked TRUSTED, and it carries that verdict's numbers (precision, recall, judged n, protocol and verdict event ids) so a reader sees how often this signal is right without leaving the row. Today that is `corrections` alone. (3) THE HASH IS THE EVIDENCE: sha256 over canonical {version, signal, scope, sorted evidence ids} — not the cutoff, not prose, not a branch. New evidence means a new candidate; a rejected candidate stays suppressed until its evidence set changes, which is exactly when its hash does. (4) APPROVAL BINDS TO THE EXACT CANDIDATE: approve, reject and revert re-derive candidates from the current log and refuse when the hash is no longer derivable, naming the hash that replaced it. Revert is a new event that ends an approval; nothing is erased or rewritten. (5) SURFACES: `sofar suggest [slug|--all] --dry-run [--json]` derives and prints, writing nothing; persistence is always an explicit verb — `suggest record|approve|reject|revert <hash>`; `suggest list` shows every candidate with its full history. `sofar tune` stays detection-only. No MCP tool and no digest section: the operator asks for suggestions, they are never pushed into every session's context. (6) MINIMUM EVIDENCE 3 instances in scope — one correction is ordinary work, a cluster is a pattern — and at most 10 open candidates per initiative. (7) PROTECTED FLOOR: the set of things a suggestion may ever change is today EMPTY (a loss row changes nothing), and log integrity, session routing, standing constraints, evaluator integrity, permissions and release policy are never in it. (8) Offline replay (context size, information preservation) is DEFERRED with a rule, because no trusted detector yields a candidate that changes injected context: no candidate kind that changes what is injected may ship before that check exists.
payload.over: Candidates that name a cause or a fix (2.1's rule 3 forbids the detector; inheriting it in the proposal would launder the same guess); one candidate per finding (27 rows in this repo's own record); hashing the cutoff (every new event would churn every hash and defeat rejection suppression); a digest section or an MCP tool for suggestions (r1-fixes 2.1/2.4 are cutting injected bytes and tool schemas); building the replay check now against no candidate that needs it.
payload.rule: A suggestion carries the 2.2 trust numbers of the detector that produced it, names no cause and proposes no change; approval binds to the candidate hash and is refused once the evidence set moves.

# 1. §Suggestions section, right after the Tune section.
anchor = "## Cursor primitive (sync-ready contract)"
section = """## Suggestions (self-improve — propose-only; a loss row is never a fix)
`sofar suggest [slug|--all] --dry-run [--json]` derives LOSS ROWS from the
detectors the 2.2 precision protocol marked TRUSTED and prints them, writing
nothing. `--list` shows the recorded ones with their history. Persisting is
always an explicit verb: `sofar suggest-record|-approve|-reject|-revert
<candidate>`, one event each. There is no MCP tool and no digest section — the
operator asks for suggestions; they are never pushed into every session.

**A candidate.** `{candidate, signal, scope (one initiative), evidence, count,
cutoff, engine, detector_version, trust}`. It names no cause and proposes no
change: `corrections` proves the record was fixed N times, not why, so the
fix, its predicted gain, its falsifier and its budget belong to Phase 3, which
consumes approved rows. `trust` carries what 2.2 measured about the signal —
precision, recall, the judged n, and the protocol and verdict event ids — so a
reader sees how often it is right without leaving the row.

**Trust gates emission.** A candidate exists only for a signal the 2.2
protocol trusts (today `corrections` alone: precision 0.97, recall 0.53).
Every other detector stays report-only in §Tune, and adding one REQUIRES a
re-run of that protocol on a fresh held-out corpus. A detector the corpus gate
left UNKNOWN proposes nothing, and a signal needs at least 3 instances in
scope — one correction is ordinary work, a cluster is a pattern.

**The hash is the evidence.** `candidate` is sha256 over `{version, signal,
scope, sorted evidence}` — not the cutoff, not prose, not a branch name. New
evidence is a NEW candidate. That is what makes approval bind to the exact one
and keeps a rejected row suppressed until its evidence actually moves.

**Transitions are append-only.** `record` refuses a candidate the record no
longer derives, one already recorded, one whose identical evidence was already
rejected, and any beyond 10 awaiting a verdict in an initiative. `approve` is
refused once the evidence set has moved, naming the candidate that replaced
it. `reject` and `revert` require a reason. `revert` ends an approval with a
new event — stale or not, because an approval that cannot be undone is a trap
— and erases nothing. Suggestions are deliberately NOT folded into
InitiativeState, and they are excluded from drift (commit-attribution D18): a
row that changes nothing cannot stale a next action.

**The protected floor.** The set of things a suggestion may ever change is
today EMPTY, and log integrity, session routing, standing constraints,
evaluator integrity, permissions and release policy are never in it. No
candidate kind that changes what is INJECTED may ship before the offline
replay check (context size, information preservation) exists.

"""

payload.because: Audit S4 asks for a frozen supervisor and evaluator outside the candidate's write/control surface with the whole measurement path pinned, known-good/known-bad controls, and tamper fixtures — and says to pick a mechanism that actually enforces the boundary and to state remaining limits honestly. sandbox-exec is the only enforcement available to this uid without sudo, and its behaviour was tested rather than assumed. Pinning by content hash rather than by commit alone catches uncommitted edits in the live runner tree; pinning only the files the evaluator uses lets it run while a peer's round-orchestration edits are dirty. Sandboxing every execution of candidate code, not just the agent, closes the `sofar init`, pack-time build and agent-authored build-script paths that a checksum never sees. The self-test at every run turns the isolation claim into a per-run measurement, in the same spirit as session-driver D8's settings read-back.
payload.chose: 3.1 contract — the FROZEN EVALUATOR, settled before code. (1) SEPARATE REPO AND PROCESS: the evaluator lives in ~/IO/sofar-evaluator (own local git, bun + TypeScript, zero deps), never in sofar (the candidate's repo) and never in handoff-bench (the live round-1 runner a peer session edits). Results land under ~/IO/bench-cells/evaluator/<run>/, written only by the evaluator process. No sofar binary — candidate or installed — ever interprets a result (audit S4: the candidate may be the supervising binary). (2) THE MEASUREMENT PATH IS PINNED, NOT TRUSTED: PIN.json names the handoff-bench commit plus sha256 of every file the evaluator uses (hidden-tests/** incl. vendor fixtures, CHAIN-A.md, runner/lib/{agents,arms,billing,cell,chain,mcp,paths,proc}.ts, runner package.json + bun.lock), the skeleton commit efc0137 and its tree hash, the chain-A reference commit 65a98ca, the sandbox profiles' hashes, and the tool versions (bun, node, claude, macOS, sandbox-exec present). Every run re-verifies all of it and REFUSES (exit 2, a refusal record, nothing else) on any hash mismatch, a missing or added file, a dirty working copy of a pinned path, or a tool version change — naming the first offender. (3) THE CANDIDATE RUNS INSIDE A KERNEL SANDBOX, AND SO DOES EVERY BYTE OF ITS CODE: macOS sandbox-exec (Seatbelt) profile `candidate.sb`: (allow default), (deny file-write*) with an allow-list {the cell directory, the bench agent profile ~/.bench/claude-config, ~/.local/state/sofar, /private/tmp, /private/var/folders, /dev}, (deny file-read*) on {hidden-tests, ~/IO/bench-sealed, the chain-A reference, the evaluator results, the evaluator repo}, and (deny process-exec /bin/launchctl). It applies to the agent (`claude` reached through a PATH shim that exec's sandbox-exec), to the candidate `sofar` (its bin entry IS such a shim), to `sofar init` during cell setup, and to the candidate's own build during `pack`. The agent-written app's `bun install`/`build` and the hidden-test run execute under a second profile `score.sb` (writes: the cell repo, tmp, the junit outfile only) because an agent-authored build script is candidate code too. (4) ISOLATION IS MEASURED AT EVERY RUN: before any launch the evaluator runs a self-test inside candidate.sb — write hidden-tests, write results, read harness.ts, read bench-sealed, exec launchctl must ALL fail with EPERM and a write into the cell must succeed — and refuses to launch otherwise. Verified 2026-09-16 on macOS 27.0: write allow-list, rm/mv/chmod, symlink escape, sealed read and nested profiles all enforce. (5) CANDIDATE IDENTITY IS THE ARTIFACT, NOT THE BRANCH: `pack` exports one git commit with `git archive`, builds and `npm pack`s sofar.sh inside the sandbox, and names the candidate `cand-<sha256(tarball)[0:12]>`; the result carries the commit, the tarball hash and the package version; the install lives under bench-cells/evaluator/candidates (write-denied to the candidate). (6) CONTROLS PROVE THE EVALUATOR CAN SEE PASS AND FAIL: per pin, the requested sessions' hidden tests are run against the chain-A reference (every test must pass) and the skeleton (each session must fail at least one test); a candidate score is refused until both controls hold for the current pin. (7) SCORES ARE READ FROM THE TRUSTED PROCESS, CROSS-CHECKED: the junit file is written to a random per-run name, parsed by the evaluator, and must agree with the `bun test` exit code and stdout summary; a filter that ran zero tests is `no_tests_ran`, never a pass; disagreement is `score_inconsistent` and refused. The agent's own text is never a score. (8) EVERY LAUNCH IS RECORDED BEFORE IT HAPPENS: attempts.jsonl gets a row before and after each agent launch with usage and reported cost, the seed 3.2's durable ledger sums; a billing/limit signal (bench-refresh D14 patterns) stops the run with exit 3. (9) THE HOLDOUT IS UNREACHABLE BY CONSTRUCTION: the evaluator re-execs ITSELF under `evaluator.sb`, which denies reading ~/IO/bench-sealed, so the development loop cannot touch chain B even by bug. (10) STATED LIMITS: everything runs as one uid, so the boundary covers the process tree the evaluator launches and nothing the operator starts outside it; sandbox-exec is deprecated by Apple though enforced today; the candidate can read most of the machine (only sealed paths are read-denied) and reach the network; a candidate could still plant persistence through IPC the profile does not name. The one handoff-bench change is `BENCH_SOFAR_PREFIX` as an env override of the pinned prefix in runner/lib/paths.ts, default unchanged, so the live round is untouched (bench-refresh D5).
payload.over: A checksum plus a final diff of hidden-tests/*.ts (the audit's S4 straw man); chmod a-w on the evaluator tree (same uid can chmod back); a second unix account (real isolation, but needs sudo and an interactive setup the operator has not granted — kept as a later hardening); putting the evaluator inside the sofar repo or its packages (the candidate's write surface); reusing the round-1 runner's run.ts/ledger.ts/modes.ts (dirty in a peer's tree, and its caps are 3.2's job); swapping the contents of ~/.bench/sofar-0.32.0 to point at a candidate (audit S6: never swap the installed sofar under a running benchmark); trusting the junit file alone (the app under test runs inside the same score sandbox and could write it).
payload.rule: Every execution of candidate code — the agent, the candidate sofar, its build, the agent-written app's build and tests — runs under the evaluator's sandbox profile, and a result is written only by the evaluator process after the pin, the sandbox self-test and both controls hold; never score a candidate with any sofar binary or from any text the agent wrote.

payload.because: D9 §4 says isolation is measured, not assumed, and the measurement found the mechanism's limits before any launch: nested-apply refusal and symlink-form mismatch. Both are properties of the OS, not of this code, so they belong in the record for every later session that touches a profile. A self-test that can pass while the sandbox was never applied is worse than none, so the allow probe and the apply-failure classification are now load-bearing and unit-tested.
payload.chose: D9 §9 REVISED (the evaluator's own kernel sandbox is dropped) and two measured Seatbelt facts fixed into the evaluator. Measured 2026-09-16 on macOS 27.0 with /usr/bin/sandbox-exec: (a) a profile can be applied inside an existing sandbox ONLY when it is byte-identical to the one in force — outer `(allow default)` with any different inner profile, or any two different profiles in either order, fail with `sandbox_apply: Operation not permitted` (exit 71); identical text nests fine. (b) Profile paths match the RESOLVED vnode path only: an entry naming `/var/folders/…` never matches a write that reaches `/private/var/folders/…`, while an entry naming `/private/var/folders` matches writes spelled either way. Consequences built: the evaluator process is not re-exec'd under a holdout-denying profile (it would break every candidate, pack and score sandbox inside it, which is exactly how the first controls run recorded `build_failed` for both reference and skeleton); the holdout stays unreachable by the candidate through its kernel profile, and by the evaluator through test/holdout.test.ts, which pins that every mention of the sealed path in evaluator source is a deny-list entry, a probe target or the definition. Every path is realpath'd before it enters a profile. The self-test judges a probe from exit code AND what it left behind, and a `sandbox_apply` failure is reported as "could not be applied" for every probe rather than counted as a successful deny — the first self-test passed ten deny probes vacuously for that reason and was caught only by the one allow probe. The scorer throws (never records a score) when its sandbox could not be applied. The self-test fixture lives on a real path under the evaluator store, not under tmp, which every profile allows.
payload.over: Keeping the evaluator's own profile and applying candidate profiles identical to it (the evaluator must write results the candidate must not); enforcing the holdout ban with chmod (same uid); trusting a deny probe's non-zero exit without checking why it failed.
payload.rule: Never apply a second, different Seatbelt profile inside a sandboxed process, and never put a symlinked path form in a profile — realpath every entry — and treat a `sandbox_apply` failure as "no isolation", never as a deny.

payload.text: macOS Seatbelt (/usr/bin/sandbox-exec), measured 2026-09-16 on macOS 27.0: (1) nesting works only with a byte-identical profile — applying any different profile inside a sandboxed process fails `sandbox_apply: Operation not permitted`, exit 71; so a tool that wraps children in sandbox-exec must itself run unsandboxed (a Claude Code Bash sandbox or an outer profile breaks it). (2) Profile paths match the resolved vnode path only: write `/private/var/folders` and `/private/tmp`, never `/var/folders` or `/tmp`, and realpath every entry. (3) `(allow default)(deny file-write*)(allow file-write* (subpath …))` is a working write allow-list; `(deny file-read* (subpath …))` seals reads; rm/mv/chmod/symlink-escape are all caught. # sofar-evaluator

The frozen evaluator of the sofar self-improve loop (self-improve 3.1; contract in
self-improve D9, amended by D10). It scores a CANDIDATE — one commit of the sofar
repo, packed into an artifact — on the Boopada benchmark workload, and it is
built so that the candidate cannot influence its own score.

It lives in its own repo and process: never inside sofar (the candidate's write
surface), never inside handoff-bench (the live round runner). Results are written
only by this process, under `~/IO/bench-cells/evaluator/`.

## What "frozen" means here

1. **The measurement path is pinned by content.** `PIN.json` holds the sha256 of
   every file the evaluator executes or reads from handoff-bench (the chain-A
   hidden tests and vendor fixtures, `CHAIN-A.md`, the runner library modules it
   imports), the skeleton and chain-A reference commits by tree hash, and the
   tool versions (bun, node, npm, claude, macOS, sandbox-exec). Every command
   re-verifies all of it and refuses (exit 2) on a modified, missing or added
   file, a dirty pinned path, a moved tree or a changed tool — naming the first.
2. **Every byte of candidate code runs inside a kernel sandbox.** macOS Seatbelt
   via `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec`. The candidate profile is a write ALLOW-list (the
   run's cells, the bench agent profile, the candidate sofar's private state,
   tmp and caches) plus a read DENY-list (hidden tests, `bench-sealed`, the
   chain-A reference, the runner, this repo, the run's results) and no
   `launchctl`. It applies to the agent (`claude` is reached through a shim on
   PATH), to the candidate `sofar` (its bin entry IS a shim), to `sofar init` at
   cell setup, and to the candidate's own `npm ci` / `npm pack` when it is
   packed. The agent-written app's `bun install`, `bun run build` and the hidden
   test run execute under a second, write-only-into-the-repo profile.
3. **Isolation is measured at every run.** Before any launch, eleven probes run
   inside the real profile: writes and reads that must fail, one write that must
   succeed, `launchctl` that must not exec. A probe is judged by exit code AND by
   what it left behind, and a failed `sandbox_apply` is reported as "no
   isolation", never as a deny. `evaluator selftest` runs the same probes on demand.
4. **Controls prove the evaluator can see pass and fail.** Per pin and per
   session, the hidden tests must pass on the chain-A reference and fail on the
   skeleton before any candidate is scored.
5. **Scores come from the trusted process, cross-checked.** The junit file (random
   per-run name) is reconciled with `bun test`'s exit code and its own summary; a
   filter that ran no tests is `no_tests_ran`, a disagreement is
   `score_inconsistent`, and neither is ever a pass. Nothing the agent writes is a score.
6. **Candidate identity is the artifact.** `pack` exports one commit with
   `git archive`, builds and packs `sofar.sh` inside the sandbox, and names the
   candidate `cand-<sha256(tarball)[0:12]>`; results carry commit, tarball hash
   and version.
7. **Every launch is recorded before it happens** (`results/attempts.jsonl`, with
   usage and reported cost afterwards) — the seed of the 3.2 spend ledger. A
   billing/limit signal (bench-refresh D14 patterns) stops the run with exit 3.

## Commands

    bun evaluator.ts pin write            # (re)pin the measurement path; commit PIN.json
    bun evaluator.ts pin check            # exit 2 with the offenders if it does not hold
    bun evaluator.ts selftest             # the eleven probes against the real protected paths
    bun evaluator.ts pack --repo ~/IO/sofar --ref <commit>
    bun evaluator.ts controls --sessions [redacted]
    bun evaluator.ts run --candidate cand-xxxxxxxxxxxx --sessions [redacted] \
        [--arm claude-sofar] [--reps 1] [--model opus] [--effort high] [--timeout-min 60] \
        [--run <name>] [--dry-run] [--allow-dirty-evaluator]
    bun evaluator.ts verify <result.json>  # sha256 sidecar check
    bun test                               # tamper fixtures: pin diffs, sandbox probes, forged scores, holdout guard

Exit codes: 0 ok · 1 crash · 2 refusal (pin, dirty evaluator, controls, self-test)
· 3 billing/limit stop.

## Layout of the store (`~/IO/bench-cells/evaluator/`)

    candidates/<id>/          sofar.sh.tgz, node_modules/sofar.sh (the install), candidate.json
    candidates/by-commit/     commit → id pointers
    controls/<pin-hash>/      reference/ and skeleton/ clones, per-session [redacted] logs
    runs/<run>/cells/         the only tree the candidate may write
    runs/<run>/shims/         claude + sofar shims and the candidate prefix the runner is pointed at
    runs/<run>/sandbox/       the exact profiles used (hashed into results)
    runs/<run>/results/       run.json, selftest.json, attempts.jsonl, <arm>-r<n>-<S>.json (+ .sha256), agent raw output, build/test logs
    runs/refusals/            one record per refusal

## Stated limits (D9 §10, D10)

- Everything runs as one uid. The boundary covers the process tree this
  evaluator launches and nothing the operator starts outside it. A second unix
  account would be stronger and needs sudo; not done.
- `sandbox-exec` is deprecated by Apple; it is enforced on macOS 27.0 today, and
  the self-test is what says so on the current machine.
- Seatbelt refuses to apply a profile that differs from one already in force
  (exit 71). So the evaluator process itself is NOT sandboxed (an outer profile
  would break every inner one), and running the evaluator from inside another

- Profile paths must be resolved paths; the code realpaths every entry.
- The candidate may read most of the machine (only the sealed set is

- The runner modules imported from handoff-bench are pinned by content, and the
  one change made there for this evaluator is `BENCH_SOFAR_PREFIX` as an env
  override of the pinned sofar install (default unchanged).

payload.chose: 3.2 contract — the DURABLE SPEND LEDGER, settled before code. (1) ONE append-only JSONL across every run: ~/IO/bench-cells/evaluator/ledger.jsonl, written only by the evaluator process (inside the candidate's write-denied store). Kinds: pack, controls, score (time only, no model), launch_intent (BEFORE a launch), launch_outcome (after: ok, timed out, exit, ms, turns, tokens, reported cost), launch_lost (an intent the process never closed, written on resume or reconcile), refusal, stop. The run-local results/attempts.jsonl stays as a filtered copy. (2) EVERY ATTEMPT COSTS SOMETHING, never zero: a launch is REPORTED (claude -p's total_cost_usd), UNKNOWN (an outcome with no usage) or OPEN (an intent with no outcome — the evaluator died, the machine slept, the operator killed it). Unknown and open attempts are charged at the next-session estimate (`--next-session-usd`, default $8, the same headroom figure the round-1 runner uses) in every cap check and reported apart from reported spend, with their counts. Controls, packs and scoring count as attempts with time but no model cost — the whole improvement cost (self-improve D1 addition C) includes them. (3) CAPS, checked before EVERY launch and stated on the run's stream: per-run `--max-usd` (default $20) on the run's cumulative spend across restarts; the bench-refresh D17 rolling caps — 7-day $450 and 5-hour $150 — over Claude spend computed the runner's way (claude-code arms, reported cost, ended inside the window) over the round-1 ledgers PLUS this ledger, so the evaluator's spend counts against the operator's half-limit; `--max-launches` (default sessions × reps, lost attempts included) bounds no-progress retries. A cap hit is a PAUSE (exit 4, a `stop` row with the reason, resumable), a billing/limit signal is a STOP (exit 3, D14), and neither is ever silent. (4) RESTART-SAFE: `run --run <id> --resume` re-verifies pin, controls and the sandbox self-test, skips every (rep, session) that already has a result, closes open intents with launch_lost, resets the cell repo to its last bench commit (git reset --hard + clean, as the round-1 runner does) before relaunching, and charges the lost attempt. (5) LIMITS STATED: the round-1 runner does not read this ledger, so ITS caps exclude evaluator spend while the evaluator's include both; costs are what the agent reports on a subscription (API-equivalent, not billed); only claude-code is metered here.
